questions.prompt: You are about to write a model for a control loop. Which quantities become the states?
questions.explanation: A state is a stored quantity. You need its initial value, and its derivative is what the differential equation gives you. An input is chosen by the actuator or imposed from outside, so it is \(u\), not \(x\). The reference is a signal the controller compares against the measurement. A disturbance is an extra input, not a state, unless the disturbance itself has dynamics you decide to model.

questions.prompt: A length scale is \(0.4\ \mathrm{m}\) and a velocity scale is \(2\ \mathrm{m/s}\). The time scale formed from those two is
questions.explanation: Time is length over velocity: \(0.4/2 = 0.2\) s. Multiplying gives \(0.8\ \mathrm{m^2/s}\), which is not a time. Dividing the velocity by the length gives \(5\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\), a rate, not the time scale.

questions.prompt: A motor's electrical transient dies in a fraction of a millisecond. The loop you care about moves a load over several seconds. A useful model of that loop
questions.explanation: The loop never sees the electrical spike, so that state can be replaced by the algebraic gain it settles to. Keeping it is not free: it adds a fast pole the controller will not move. Dropping the mechanical states drops the motion the loop is for. A model with no states cannot accumulate a position or a speed.
questions.figure_alt: A curve used only as a picture of a transient.
options: keeps every electrical state, because more states are always safer
can replace the electrical transient by the gain it settles to
drops the mechanical states, because they are slow

questions.prompt: A shaft turns at 1500 revolutions per minute. Its speed in radians per second is
questions.explanation: One revolution is \(2\pi\) radians, and a minute is 60 seconds: \(1500 \times 2\pi/60 = 157.1\). Dividing by 60 alone gives 25 revolutions per second, still not radians. Multiplying by \(2\pi\) and forgetting the 60 leaves the per-minute number. Using \(\pi\) instead of \(2\pi\) is half a revolution.

questions.prompt: Why divide a differential equation through by its scales before you decide a term is small?
questions.explanation: After scaling, each term is a number. A term near 0.01 can be dropped beside a term near 1. Before scaling, a term in newtons cannot be called smaller than a term in meters. Scaling does not set every initial condition to 1, and it does not swap the time constant with the gain.

So the terms are pure numbers and can be compared with each other
So the time constant becomes the DC gain

questions.prompt: A sensor produces \(0.025\ \mathrm{V}\) per millimeter. A motion of 36 mm produces a voltage of
questions.explanation: Multiply the sensitivity by the motion: \(0.025 \times 36 = 0.9\) V. Dividing the motion by the sensitivity gives 1440, which is a count of how many 0.025 V steps fit in 36, not a voltage. Adding the two numbers mixes volts-per-millimeter with millimeters.

questions.prompt: One stored quantity moves on a 0.04 s scale. Another moves on a 6.4 s scale. The ratio of the slow scale to the fast scale is
questions.explanation: The ratio is \(6.4/0.04 = 160\). The product \(0.256\) is a time squared over a time, not a ratio. The reciprocal \(0.00625\) compares them in the other order.
questions.figure_alt: A curve used only as a picture of a transient.

questions.prompt: The loop must hold a constant reference with no steady error. The model used to design that loop should
questions.explanation: A constant error goes to zero only if something in the loop integrates it. Dropping that integrator makes the design model predict an error the hardware will not have, or hide an error the hardware will have. The high-frequency slope matters for stability margins, not for the constant error. The sensor is inside the loop, so its gain belongs in the model.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 216 120" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a free integrator</title><line x1="24" y1="56" x2="60" y2="56"/><polygon points="60,56 53.6,58.7 53.6,53.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><rect x="60" y="34" width="84" height="44" rx="4" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.10"/><text x="102" y="60" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">integrator</text><line x1="144" y1="56" x2="180" y2="56"/><polygon points="180,56 173.6,58.7 173.6,53.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="184" y="60" text-anchor="start" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">y</text></svg>
options: omit every integrator, to keep the order low
replace the plant by its high-frequency slope
ignore the sensor, because the sensor is not the plant
keep a free integrator if the error is supposed to vanish

questions.prompt: A mass is \(1.5\ \mathrm{kg}\) and its acceleration is \(4\ \mathrm{m/s^2}\). The force that goes with those two numbers is
questions.explanation: Force is mass times acceleration: \(1.5 \times 4 = 6\) N. Adding gives 5.5 and mixes kilograms with meters per second squared. Dividing gives \(2.67\), which is not a force. Multiplying by \(9.81\) as well would be the weight of a different problem.

questions.prompt: A one-state model is \(\dot{y} = 2.4 - 0.3y\). Linearization will be about the resting point. The resting value of \(y\) is
questions.explanation: At rest the derivative is zero, so \(0.3y = 2.4\) and \(y = 8\). The product \(0.72\) multiplies the two coefficients. The difference \(2.1\) subtracts them. Neither is a root of the right-hand side.
questions.figure_alt: A curve used only as a picture of a transient.

questions.prompt: A step test on a one-pole plant reaches about 63% of its steady change at 3.5 s. The time constant you would identify is
questions.explanation: For a first-order rise, 63% of the step happens at one time constant, so the identified \(\tau\) is 3.5 s. Half of that, 1.75 s, is closer to the halfway time \(\tau\ln 2\). Twice 3.5 is two time constants.
questions.figure_alt: A curve used only as a picture of a transient.

questions.prompt: Equilibria of \(\dot{y} = -2y + u\) with the constant input \(u = 5\). The resting \(y\) is
questions.explanation: Set \(\dot{y} = 0\): \(2y = 5\), so \(y = 2.5\). The product \(10\) and the difference \(3\) are not roots. Leaving the input as the state forgets the \(-2y\) term.
questions.figure_alt: A curve used only as a picture of a transient.
